summary: Discovery focused on SilverGate's need for dedicated GPU capacity for LLM inference: predictable performance, VPC network isolation, burst handling for peak trading hours, and compliance (SOC2, KMS). Redwood AE + SE discussed architecture options (Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private), autoscaling and burst strategies, benchmark plan, and next steps to run a POC.
topics: POC benchmark plan and success metrics
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-12 16:00 PST · 52 min
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood Solutions); Laura Kim (Head of AI, SilverGate), Marcus Diaz (Infra), Anjali Rao (CTO), David Lin (SRE)

[00:00] Ethan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood Inference, with Priya our solutions engineer — how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Laura: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in. Quick note, we're on a tight timeline — want to have something running for internal demos by mid December.
[00:15] Priya: Great, we'll try to keep this practical. Can I do a quick round — current stack and what you're trying to solve with model serving?
[00:23] Marcus: Sure. We run a mix of in-house transformers for document processing and an upstream LLM for assistant features. Right now inference is on cloud VMs with GPUs but it's ad hoc; we need more predictable throughput and isolation for regulated workloads.
[00:35] Anjali: Also cost spikes during market open are killing us. We need reserved capacity and a burst strategy that doesn't overcommit.
[00:45] Ethan: Got it — sounds like a Dedicated capacity conversation. Do you currently use any managed endpoints? Any constraints around data residency or private network?
[00:54] Laura: We have two compliance requirements — SOC2 type II and customer data must not leave our VPC for certain flows. We're open to a hosted service for low-sensitivity traffic, but critical inference must be on dedicated isolated GPUs.
[01:05] Priya: Good context. A few follow-ups — target p99 latency, tokens per second, and concurrency expectations?
[01:12] David: For our assistant use-case p99 should be under 350ms for 256-token responses, and we want to support bursts up to ~200 concurrent requests during market open. Baseline sustained concurrency is about 40 qps.
[01:25] Priya: Ok that's helpful. Do you have preferred models or quantization? We often recommend quantized variants for cost, but that changes latency/quality tradeoffs.
[01:34] Laura: We'll need fidelity close to the largest open models — we care about hallucination rates more than tiny latency wins. Also we have to run some privacy-sensitive reranking models, so those must stay private.
[01:45] Ethan: Makes sense. For Dedicated, you can reserve a set of GPU nodes in a VPC-backed deployment. You can configure autoscaling and burst cushions; we also do automated fallbacks to smaller model variants if needed.
[01:56] Marcus: How does the burst cushion work? We can't spin up GPUs in real-time during peak, so we need a reserve plus some burst from shared capacity.
[02:05] Priya: Two approaches — 1) Dedicated reserved pool sized for baseline plus some headroom, and 2) optionally enable a throttle/burst policy that lets requests overflow to a shared or lower-tier pool for non-sensitive calls. For private-only workloads we recommend reserved with a carefully sized burst buffer (e.g., 15-30% extra headroom) and request queuing/priority.
[02:22] Anjali: Can you do on-prem private deployment for fully air-gapped?
[02:26] Ethan: Yes, Redwood Private supports on-prem or customer-managed infra; that's a different procurement track but technically possible.
[02:32] Laura: We need to understand pricing — committed reserved vs pay-as-you-go.
[02:36] Ethan: We'll send a pricing sheet, but high-level: reserved monthly commits for Dedicated offer much lower per-token cost than hosted. We can size a 3-node GPU cluster as an example for your workload.
[02:46] Marcus: On autoscaling — what's the granularity? Node-level or pod-level? How fast can it react to spikes?
[02:52] Priya: Autoscaling operates at the request routing and worker pool level. Node-level scale-out has startup time (minutes) but we have warm pools and fast pre-warm strategies. For latency-sensitive spikes we recommend a hybrid: keep a baseline of warm workers and use dynamic routing to lower-cost nodes for non-critical traffic.
[03:10] Laura: For NFRs, we need KMS integration, customer-managed keys, and audit logs for every inference.
[03:16] Ethan: We support KMS/HSM integrations and full audit logs, plus role-based access control and SSO/SAML. We'll attach SOC2 and our security whitepaper.
[03:24] David: On networking, we need VPC peering and control over egress; can Redwood peer to our AWS account?
[03:31] Priya: Yes, Dedicated can be deployed into a customer VPC or we do VPC peering from our control plane. For fully private we can do private networking and no public egress.
[03:40] Anjali: Any constraints on model size or memory per GPU? We run some 40B models.
[03:45] Priya: We support up to 70B on multi-GPU shards; for 40B you can do single-GPU depending on memory/profile, or use tensor-parallel across nodes. We'll validate in the POC.
[03:58] Ethan: Let's talk benchmarks — what are the key success metrics for the POC?
[04:02] Laura: 1) p99 latency <350ms for 256 tokens, 2) sustain 40 qps for baseline, 3) handle 200 concurrent burst requests with graceful degradation, 4) identical output quality to our current model within a small delta on eval prompts.
[04:17] Priya: Good. We'll propose a POC with a 72-hour benchmark run covering those scenarios, plus a mixed workload test (streaming + reranking).
[04:26] Marcus: Would we be able to run a small production shadow traffic test?
[04:29] Ethan: Yes — after initial benchmarks we can run shadow and then a canary rollout.
[04:33] Laura: Security question — how long do you retain logs and transcripts? We need to ensure data retention policies can be configured per customer.
[04:41] Priya: Retention is configurable; we can disable transcript storage for certain routes, and audit logs can be exported to your SIEM.
[04:46] David: Does Redwood support token-level cost breakdowns in the console?
[04:49] Ethan: Yep, Console shows token breakdowns per route/model and per API key. Cost controls and quotas are available.
[04:55] Anjali: Any other customers in fintech doing dedicated? References would help.
[04:59] Ethan: We have several mid-market banks using Dedicated — we'll share references.
[05:05] -- 05:30 short break as people join back --
[05:30] Priya: Back to architecture, in Dedicated we recommend configuring two classes of nodes: inference-optimized (low latency) and throughput-optimized (higher batching). You can route trading-critical traffic to inference-optimized nodes.
[05:47] Marcus: How do you manage KV cache / prefix caching across requests? We currently use a Redis-backed cache in front.
[05:53] Priya: Redwood supports KV cache and prefix caching at the runtime level; it can be local to the worker or a shared cache; for cross-node consistency we integrate with Redis or in-memory sync. We'll propose options in the POC runbook.
[06:08] Laura: About model upgrades — we need rollback and canary deploys.
[06:12] Ethan: Rollouts are supported — canary, A/B, and automatic rollback policies. You can pin model versions per route.
[06:19] Anjali: So what's high level lead time to provision a Dedicated cluster?
[06:23] Priya: For cloud Dedicated it's typically a few business days to provision reserved nodes once contract signed; if you want on-prem it can take weeks. Warm pool setup and initial model loading add some time to run live benchmarks.
[06:34] Marcus: That timeline works. Regarding cost, could you ballpark a 3x A100 equivalent 3-node monthly commit?
[06:41] Ethan: We'll send exact numbers, but ballpark to inform sizing — reserved is materially cheaper than cloud on-demand. We'll include an apples-to-apples cost model in the proposal.
[06:51] Laura: We may have procurement questions around indemnity and data handling.
[06:55] Ethan: We can share standard enterprise T&Cs and a data protection addendum.
[07:01] Priya: For the POC, we'd recommend: 1) 3-node dedicated cluster sized for your baseline, 2) one throughput-optimized node for mixed workloads, 3) configure a 20% burst cushion, and 4) we'll run our 72-hour benchmark including 200 concurrent burst tests.
[07:17] David: Sounds reasonable. How about telemetry and tracing hooks?
[07:21] Priya: We provide per-request tracing IDs, and integration with OpenTelemetry and your tracing backend is possible.
[07:28] Liam: I'll also follow up with a short architecture diagram and the high-level network flow doc.
[07:33] Laura: Please include SOC2 report and a short security deck.
[07:36] Ethan: Will do. Any blockers we haven't covered?
[07:40] Marcus: Only one — we need to validate model reproducibility; outputs must match within tolerances.
[07:45] Priya: We'll include an eval harness and metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, custom scoring) in the benchmark.
[07:52] Anjali: What's the proposed timeline for POC start? We said week of 11/22 — procurement needs a proposal soon.
[07:59] Ethan: We'll aim to send pricing and POC plan by 11/15 so procurement can move.
[08:05] Laura: On legal, we may need SOC2 and DPA before signing.
[08:09] Ethan: Understood, we'll include those.
[08:12] -- Transcript continues with demo/technical clarifications --
[20:00] Priya: (deep dive) For model parallelism we use a combination of tensor and pipeline parallelism depending on the model; kernel selection optimizes for latency.
[20:20] Marcus: Any constraints for continuous batching impacting cold-start latency?
[20:25] Priya: Continuous batching is tuned per route; for critical traffic we reduce batching window and favor low-latency kernels. For throughput jobs we increase batch sizes.
[30:10] David: During the POC can we test with our private dataset and meet privacy guarantees?
[30:15] Ethan: Yes, PII can be filtered and you can use private-only routes. We can also disable logging for those routes.
[35:02] Laura: Are there data residency controls? We operate across US and EU — some customers require EU-only processing.
[35:09] Priya: You can pin routes to region and Dedicated nodes to regions; for EU-only processing we can ensure compute stays in EU regions.
[40:00] Anjali: For the 200 concurrent burst — do you recommend graceful degradation strategies?
[40:05] Priya: Yes — priority queues, early-exit heuristics, and fallbacks to smaller model variants for non-critical requests. Also you can set per-route SLOs and reject or queue lower-priority traffic.
[45:00] Ethan: Quick recap: Redwood proposes 3-node Dedicated baseline with one throughput node, 20% burst cushion, POC 72-hour benchmark, deliverables include pricing, SOC2, network diagram, and POC runbook. Action items and owners we'll send in email.
[45:25] Laura: Good. Can you include reference customers and a short case study?
[45:29] Ethan: Yes, will attach a fintech reference.
[45:33] Marcus: Also include an example configuraton for autoscaling and queuing policies.
[45:36] Priya: We'll add that to the runbook.
[45:39] Anjali: All right — thanks.
[45:41] Ethan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and scheduling.
[45:44] Laura: Thanks, bye.
[52:00] Call ends
